competitors.name: AeroVironment, Inc. (incl. BlueHalo)
competitors.why: Sells small UAS, loitering munitions (Switchblade) and counter-UAS (BlueHalo) to the U.S. DoD and allies, the same buyers ONDS targets with Iron Drone/Sentrycs C-UAS and the acquired DZYNE ULTRA/IonStrike lines (ONDS Q2 2026 release names U.S. Air Force and Army as DZYNE customers); won the $500M-ceiling JIATF-401 C-UAS IDIQ in July 2026. Added by this lane: ONDS 10-K names no competitor.

metrics.growth_note: FY2026 includes the BlueHalo acquisition: not organic

competitors.name: Red Cat Holdings, Inc. (Teal Drones)
competitors.why: Small ISR drones (Black Widow, U.S. Army short-range reconnaissance) sold to U.S. and allied defense: competes with ONDS's tactical/ISR drone lines for the same small-UAS defense budgets. Added by this lane.

competitors.name: DroneShield Limited
competitors.why: Pure-play counter-drone (RF detection/defeat) vendor selling to military, government and critical-infrastructure buyers in the U.S., Europe and Australia, the same C-UAS demand that ONDS reports as its strongest product line (Q2 2026 release) and serves with Sentrycs (cyber-over-RF takeover) and Iron Drone Raider; DroneShield also holds a JIATF-401 contract. Added by this lane.

competitors.name: Elbit Systems Ltd.
competitors.why: Israel's largest defense prime: supplies UAS, loitering munitions and counter-UAS to the Israeli MOD/IDF, the customer region that gave ONDS about 61% of FY2025 revenue and 45% of Q2 2026 revenue (Israel-based subsidiaries OAS/Airobotics, Iron Drone, Sentrycs, 4M, Bird, Omnisys). Competes for the same Israeli defense budget at a vastly larger, mature scale; growth not comparable-stage. Added by this lane.

bottlenecks.reading: Scarce thing: deployable counter-small-drone defense (detect, take over or intercept) for militaries and sensitive sites. U.S. demand became funded and urgent: JIATF-401 was created in Aug 2025 with its own procurement authority and had committed >$600M by April 2026 ($350M for Operation Epic Fury, $100M for the 2026 World Cup), and issued a $500M-ceiling IDIQ to AeroVironment in July 2026 (ceiling, not obligation). ONDS says C-UAS drove its Q2 2026 strength. The money currently visible in these sources went to competitors; ONDS's own U.S. C-UAS awards are not evidenced here.

Paid adoption in ONDS's own numbers: revenue $50.7M FY2025 -> $50.1M Q1 2026 -> $83.8M Q2 2026; Q2 orders ~$175M and ~$105M more in Q3 to Aug 10; reported backlog ~$613M at 2026-06-30 (pro forma $757M with DZYNE and Cyberhawk) vs $68M at 2025-12-31. Much of the step-up is acquired (Sentrycs, 4M, Bird, Omnisys, World View, DZYNE...): management's pro forma same-portfolio Q2 growth is +85% YoY, a company-defined non-GAAP figure.

Market size is only from studies quoted by the issuer: C-UAS $3.1B in 2025 growing 27.2%/yr to $10.6B by 2030 and drones $83.7B (2025) to $160.6B (2030) per Grand View Research; North American C-UAS spend $6.8B by 2028; management TAM 'over $100 billion'. These are attributed studies chosen by the issuer, not independent checks; management states they 'underestimate' the market.

Demand concentration: two customers were ~55% and ~11% of FY2025 revenue; Israel is the largest revenue region (Q2 2026 $37.5M of $83.8M). ONDS's growth so far rides Israeli wartime defense demand, where Elbit and Rafael are entrenched incumbents.

Who adds capacity: DroneShield moved into a 3,000 m2 plant and started European manufacturing in June 2026; AeroVironment holds the $500M-ceiling domestic C-UAS IDIQ; the Pentagon's $1B Drone Dominance program buys ~340,000 cheap one-way attack drones in competitive fixed-price phases designed to push unit costs down. Supply is being added fast, so the shortage is likely to turn into price competition within a few years: this is a hypothesis, not a measured duration.

How long the C-UAS/drone shortage lasts is not evidenced: it depends on continuing conflicts (Israel, Ukraine, Iran operations) and on budgets after the current urgent-need spending; treat any multi-year scarcity premium as a hypothesis.

notes: fd NAMED COMPETITORS (10-K Item 1): the FY2025 10-K 'Competition' section names no competitor: for OAS it says it competes 'with other drone OEMs' on autonomy, ease of use, reliability, safety and regulation; for Ondas Networks it names categories only (public cellular, Wi-Fi, licensed narrowband radios) [fd_10k_fy2025]. All four competitors in this fragment (AVAV, RCAT, DRO.AX, ESLT) were added by this lane, each with a written reason. Private competitors not covered (no public numbers): Rafael (Drone Dome), D-Fend Solutions (cyber C-UAS, closest to Sentrycs), Skydio, Anduril, Percepto (drone-in-a-box, closest to Optimus).
fd SEGMENTS: after deconsolidating Ondas Networks, ONDS reports one operating and reportable segment [fd_10q_q2_2026]; share comparisons are therefore total-company only.

fd SHARE (hypothesis): latest quarters on own numbers: ONDS Q2 2026 revenue $83.8M (13x YoY, mostly acquired; company pro forma +85%) [fd_release_q2_2026]; AVAV Q1 FY2027 $480.5M, +5.7% YoY [fd_avav_companyfacts]; RCAT Q2 2026 $20.2M, H1 +636% YoY from a tiny base [fd_rcat_companyfacts]; DroneShield 1H 2026 A$125.8M, +74%, FY2026 outlook only +15-25% [fd_dro_1h2026]. ONDS is growing its revenue faster than every named peer, but via acquisitions; organic share gain cannot be separated from bought revenue with these sources.

fd MARGINS vs PEERS: ONDS Q2 2026 GAAP gross margin 43.1% (adjusted 50.4%) [fd_release_q2_2026] sits between hardware-heavy AVAV (~25-26%) / Elbit (~24%) and C-UAS software-rich DroneShield (~60%); RCAT is ~15%. Every named small-drone/C-UAS peer is loss-making at operating level; only mature Elbit earns ~8.5%.
fd PRICING: ONDS's unit pricing or price per system is not disclosed in the sources read; no pricing lever can be built from company data (gap).
